title: [Mouse Without Borders] Service mode: SYSTEM process leaks Token/Event/Thread handles at a constant rate (~10k handles/day)

judgment.rationale: The report provides a repeatable service-mode comparison, quantified handle growth by object type, a stable interval, and an on-demand helper restart that releases the growth. The evidence supports maintainer-side tracing, but not a confirmed root cause.
evidence: On one of two Windows 11 machines running PowerToys 0.100.2 with Mouse Without Borders service mode, the SYSTEM process grew about 105 handles per 15 minutes, in Token/Event/Thread types at a roughly 3:2:1 ratio.
The reporter says any UAC prompt restarts the helper and releases the leaked handles; the observed count otherwise grows while idle.
The second machine with the same version and settings remained near a stable handle count.
The report identifies an elevated-process handle sampler and gives repeated samples at 44 and 92 hours.
judgment.recommended_action: Profile the service/helper process lifecycle under the reported two-machine service-mode setup and attribute one leaked Token/Event/Thread set before designing a code change.

fix_assessment.rationale: No linked fix attempt covers this report. A periodic per-session worker or callback lifetime may be retaining native handles, but source review has not identified the allocator or confirmed the hypothesis.

proposed_fixes.title: Close the service-mode worker handles retained across user-session callbacks
proposed_fixes.root_cause: The periodic Token/Event/Thread growth may come from a repeated service/helper session callback that creates native handles but fails to release one complete worker set on its normal path.
plan: Reproduce the issue while recording handle type, owning process/thread, and creation stack for each growing Token/Event/Thread object; compare the affected helper session with the stable peer.
Trace the identified allocation stack to its exact Mouse Without Borders service/helper callback and audit success, cancellation, exception, and restart cleanup paths.
Use scoped SafeHandle or equivalent disposal at the owning lifecycle boundary and add a focused repeated-callback regression test that checks handle counts return to baseline.
verification: Run the same service-mode workload for multiple hours and verify Token/Event/Thread counts remain bounded in both the service and helper processes.
Verify a UAC-triggered helper restart is no longer required to reclaim handles and that mouse/keyboard sharing remains functional.

confidence.rationale: The object types, fixed rate, and helper restart strongly motivate a lifetime investigation, but the allocating call stack is not known. Focused source review found token handles in Launch.ImpersonateLoggedOnUserAndDoSomething are closed in a finally block, so that path is not established as the leak.

issue_context.summary: One service-mode Mouse Without Borders SYSTEM process accumulates a stable mix of token, event, and thread handles until the helper restarts; the other otherwise-matched PC does not.
known_information: The report names PowerToys 0.100.2, Windows 11 build 26200, per-user installation, and service mode enabled on two PCs.
The affected process grows by about 105 handles per 15 minutes; process handles and live thread count remain approximately flat.
A cancelled UAC prompt restarts the helper and releases the accumulated handles.
The reporter offers additional collection, but no diagnostic archive or stack trace is attached.
inferences: The growth is likely tied to a repeated service/helper lifecycle or callback rather than TCP connection churn, because the reported TCP connections remain established and the rate continues while idle.
A repeated native-handle ownership defect is plausible, but the measured ratio alone does not establish which call site leaks.
issue_context.analysis: The issue is already actionable for a maintainer-side reproducer: the report supplies a control machine, object-type breakdown, stable interval, and helper-restart discriminator. Asking the reporter for generic logs would not identify the leaking allocation as efficiently as a focused handle-stack capture.
initial_investigation: Read the full issue body and latest author comment; labels are Issue-Bug and Needs-Triage, with no assignee or linked fix.
Read InputSimulation.SendInputEx and the per-package catch in SocketStuff.MainTCPRoutine; the reported connection remains stable, so those paths do not establish the handle leak.
Read Launch.ImpersonateLoggedOnUserAndDoSomething: it closes both user-token handles in a finally block, which is counterevidence to attributing the leak to that helper.
No repository history result identifies a change specifically for issue 51448.

actions.label: Investigate service-mode handle leak
actions.note: A focused handle-lifecycle design investigation should follow only after the allocation stack is identified.

reproduce.title: Compare Mouse Without Borders service-mode handle lifetimes
reproduce.version_requirement: Current stable build; retain 0.100.2 only as an additional compatibility comparison
prerequisites: Two Windows 11 PCs on the same stable network, with Mouse Without Borders service mode enabled on both.
One affected-machine-equivalent and one control-machine-equivalent configuration.
A handle sampler that records object type, process/thread ownership, and allocation stacks without collecting unrelated personal data.
steps: Start both PCs with the same PowerToys build and service-mode settings; record baseline Token, Event, Thread, Process, and File handle counts for each MWB process.
Leave the machines idle and connected, sampling the same object-type counts every 15 minutes for at least 24 hours.
On the test machine, correlate each growing handle set with an allocation stack and helper session; do not trigger a UAC prompt during the observation window.
At the end, trigger and cancel a UAC prompt and record whether helper restart releases the accumulated objects.
reproduce.expected_result: Counts remain bounded on both machines, or the trace identifies the exact repeated allocation and owner responsible for the growth.
